{{Short description|Stochastic process}}
{{Technical|date=November 2021}}
In the [[probability theory|mathematical theory of probability]], a '''Doob martingale''' (named after [[Joseph L. Doob]],<ref name=Doob>
{{cite journal |last=Doob |first=J. L. |year=1940 |title=Regularity properties of certain families of chance variables |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=47 |issue=3 |pages=455–486 |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1940-047-03/S0002-9947-1940-0002052-6/S0002-9947-1940-0002052-6.pdf |doi=10.2307/1989964|jstor=1989964 |doi-access=free }}
</ref> also known as a '''Levy martingale''', named after [[Paul Lévy (mathematician)|Paul Lévy]]) is a [[stochastic process]] that approximates a given [[random variable]] and has the [[Martingale (probability theory)|martingale property]] with respect to the given [[filtration (probability theory)|filtration]]. It may be thought of as the evolving sequence of best approximations to the random variable based on information accumulated up to a certain time.

When analyzing sums, [[random walk]]s, or other additive functions of [[Statistical independence|independent random variables]], one can often apply the [[central limit theorem]], [[law of large numbers]], [[Chernoff's inequality]], [[Chebyshev's inequality]] or similar tools. When analyzing similar objects where the differences are not independent, the main tools are [[Martingale (probability theory)|martingale]]s and [[Azuma's inequality]].{{Clarify|reason=what has this para to do with Doob martingale in particular|date=May 2012}}

==Definition==
Let <math>Y</math> be any random variable with <math>\mathbb{E}[|Y|] < \infty</math>. Suppose <math>\left\{\mathcal{F}_0, \mathcal{F}_1, \dots\right\}</math> is a [[Filtration_(probability_theory)|filtration]], i.e. <math>\mathcal{F}_s \subset \mathcal{F}_t</math> when <math>s<t</math>. Define
:<math>
Z_t = \mathbb{E} [Y \mid \mathcal{F}_t],
</math>
then <math>\left\{Z_0, Z_1, \dots\right\}</math> is a [[Martingale_(probability_theory)|martingale]],<ref>
{{cite book |last=Doob |first=J. L. |year=1953 |title=Stochastic processes |location=New York |publisher=Wiley |volume=101 |page=293 }}
</ref> namely '''Doob martingale''', with respect to filtration <math>\left\{\mathcal{F}_0, \mathcal{F}_1, \dots\right\}</math>. 

To see this, note that
* <math>\mathbb{E}[|Z_t|] = \mathbb{E}[|\mathbb{E} [Y \mid \mathcal{F}_t]|] \leq \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E} [|Y| \mid \mathcal{F}_t]] =  \mathbb{E} [|Y|] < \infty</math>;
* <math>\mathbb{E}[Z_t \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1}] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E} [Y \mid \mathcal{F}_t] \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1}] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1}] = Z_{t-1}</math> as <math>\mathcal{F}_{t-1} \subset \mathcal{F}_{t}</math>.

In particular, for any sequence of random variables <math>\left\{X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\right\}</math> on probability space  <math>(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \text{P})</math> and function <math>f</math> such that <math>\mathbb{E} [ | f(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n) |] < \infty</math>, one could choose 
:<math>
	Y:=f(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)
</math>
and filtration <math>\left\{\mathcal{F}_0, \mathcal{F}_1, \dots\right\}</math> such that
:<math>
\begin{align}
\mathcal{F}_0 &:= \left\{\phi, \Omega \right\}, \\
\mathcal{F}_t &:= \sigma(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_t), \forall t \geq 1,
\end{align}
</math>

i.e. <math>\sigma</math>-algebra generated by <math>X_1, X_2, \dots, X_t</math>. Then, by definition of Doob martingale, process <math>\left\{Z_0, Z_1, \dots\right\}</math> where
:<math>
\begin{align}
Z_0 &:= \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n) \mid \mathcal{F}_0] = \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)], \\
Z_t &:= \mathbb{E} [f(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n) \mid \mathcal{F}_t] = \mathbb{E} [f(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n) \mid X_1, X_2, \dots, X_t], \forall t \geq 1
\end{align}
</math>
forms a Doob martingale. Note that <math> Z_n = f(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n) </math>. This martingale can be used to prove '''McDiarmid's inequality'''.

== McDiarmid's inequality ==

{{Main|McDiarmid's inequality}}

The Doob martingale was introduced by Joseph L. Doob in 1940 to establish [[concentration inequalities]] such as McDiarmid's inequality, which applies to functions that satisfy a ''bounded differences'' property (defined below) when they are evaluated on random independent function arguments.

A function <math>f: \mathcal{X}_1 \times \mathcal{X}_2 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_n \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> satisfies the ''bounded differences property'' if substituting the value of the <math>i</math>th coordinate <math>x_i</math> changes the value of <math>f</math> by at most <math>c_i</math>. More formally, if there are constants <math>c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n</math> such that for all <math>i\in[n]</math>, and all <math>x_1\in \mathcal{X}_1,\,x_2\in \mathcal{X}_2,\, \ldots,\, x_n \in \mathcal{X}_n</math>,
:<math>
\sup_{x_i' \in \mathcal{X}_i} \left|f(x_1, \dots, x_{i-1}, x_i, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_n) - f(x_1, \dots, x_{i-1}, x_i', x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_n)\right| \leq c_i.
</math>

{{math theorem|name=McDiarmid's Inequality<ref name="Doob" />|math_statement=
Let <math>f: \mathcal{X}_1 \times \mathcal{X}_2 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_n  \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> satisfy the bounded differences property with bounds <math>c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n</math>.

Consider independent random variables <math>X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n</math> where <math>X_i \in \mathcal{X}_i</math> for all <math>i</math>.
Then, for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>,
:<math>
\text{P}\left(f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)] \geq \varepsilon\right)
\leq
\exp \left(-\frac{2 \varepsilon^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2} \right),
</math>
:<math>
\text{P}(f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)] \leq -\varepsilon)
\leq
\exp \left(-\frac{2 \varepsilon^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2}\right),
</math>
and as an immediate consequence,
:<math>
\text{P}(|f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) - \mathbb{E}[f(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)]| \geq \varepsilon)
\leq
2 \exp \left(-\frac{2 \varepsilon^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2}\right).
</math>
}}
